summary:
ShroudX is the interactive live web platform for uncovering real celestial motion across NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey. Built with a Python/FastAPI backend and React/Typescript frontend, ShroudX gets real level-2 SPHEREx cutouts from the NASA/IPAC IRSA Database via SIA2, groups different exposures by detector and wavelength to reduce chromatic flicker, masks bad flagged pixels, and then projects the result onto the North-up WCS sky grid.

ShroudX lets users blink aligned multi-epoch sequences, view inverse-variance weighted stacks, inspect epoch difference images with statistically thresholded residual lobes, track spectra and fitted motion vectors, and cross-match Gaia DR3 stars propagated to the observation epoch. Most importantly, it shows reliability warnings and missing-coverage points, instead of hiding them with fabricated placeholders.

Since SPHEREx surveys the sky across six detectors and 102 different infrared channels spanning from 0.75 µm to 5.00 µm, genuine motion from stars might get hidden by wavelength shifts or detector artifacts; thus, ShroudX turns multi-epoch raw survey cutouts into reproducible, reliable, verifiable, time-domain insight into observable surroundings for researchers and citizen scientists alike.
details:
What it does & how it works

Users enter sky coordinates (RA/Dec) or a target name (e.g., WISE 0855-0714, Barnard's Star) and view a multi-epoch time series of SPHEREx Level-2 cutouts as an interactive blink sequence, a stack, a signed epoch-difference image (where moving objects appear as bright/dark pairs), and a downloadable animated GIF.

  1. Epoch-aware resolution (coords.py): Resolves targets via SIMBAD/CDS or a benchmark catalog and propagates high-proper-motion positions (like WISE 0855, which has moved ~2.2 arcminutes since J2000) to the 2026.0 SPHEREx epoch.
  2. Cutout ingestion & flag masking (data.py, flags.py): Fetches small cutouts from IRSA instead of multi-hundred-MB full exposures, strips the heavy PSF HDU, subtracts the ZODI zodiacal-light model, and decodes MP_* header bits to mask only genuine detector defects while preserving SOURCE pixels (bit 21).
  3. Wavelength-matched alignment (processing.py): Evaluates per-pixel wavelength from WCS-WAVE, groups exposures within one detector (1–6) and a narrow ≤ 0.10 μm window, splits revisits into > 30-day epochs, and aligns frames onto a North-up, East-left TAN WCS grid (6.15"/px) with a single shared asinh stretch.
  4. Astrometry, Gaia DR3 & mover search (motion.py, gaia.py, movers.py): Fits proper motion and parallax with χ_ν²-scaled uncertainties, cross-matches against Gaia DR3 propagated from 2016.0 to 2026.0, and runs a 5σ blind mover search with Monte Carlo false-match estimation.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Inspired by WiseView (which enabled citizen scientists to discover hundreds of brown dwarfs in WISE), ShroudX brings browser-based blinking and difference imaging to SPHEREx's 102-band infrared archive (0.75–5.00 μm)—eliminating 200+ MB FITS downloads and making every view reproducible via URL query parameters.

How it is creative

  • Solving Linear Variable Filter (LVF) flicker: Because SPHEREx's LVFs observe each exposure at a different wavelength, fixed stars change brightness between frames. Our colour-flicker experiment (experiments/flicker.py) and sliding-window selector prevent chromatic flicker from masquerading as motion.
  • Infrared + Optical synergy: Cross-matching SPHEREx against Gaia DR3 separates known optical movers (Barnard's Star, 0.00" match) from dark, infrared-only substellar objects (WISE 0855-0714, ~250 K Y-dwarf with no gaia counterpart).

Tools & Stack

  • Backend: Python 3.10+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, reproject, astroquery/pyvo, Pillow, Matplotlib, Pytest.
  • Frontend: Dependency-free single-file HTML/CSS/JS (static/index.html) and a non-root Docker container (python:3.12-slim) with an 18.10 MB bundled cache of 5 demo fields (l2b-v27) and bounded IRSA concurrency/timeouts.

Factors Considered

We designed around fast-mover catalog drift, FLAGS bitmask pitfalls, IRSA rate limits (≤ 5 workers with backoff/caching), and honest scientific reporting—pre-declaring pass/fail criteria in every validation script, reporting uncertainties on every measurement, never silently falling back to synthetic data, and warning users when < 2 epochs exist or when sigma-clipped stacking suppresses fast movers.
